title: Hebrew Education and the Schools of Skala
summary: Schools and teachers shaped the learning and cultural life of generations of Skala’s Jewish children.

## A school built by local initiative

In Skala, Hebrew education was more than a set of lessons: it helped shape a shared cultural life. The memorial book remembers a community that supported several kinds of Jewish learning, from traditional study to modern Hebrew schooling. Its accounts name the teachers, organizers, donors and students who made that education possible. ([Skala Jewish community](/communities/skala/records/mention_4d24297290f1a4fed1e56c40); [Skala](/communities/skala/records/mention_e45df50311765e6716832a1b))

The dates for the first Hebrew school do not align exactly. One record places its beginning around 1908 or 1909, while another remembers a Hebrew Tarbut school founded in 1906. A separate account credits Avi Moti Vidber with establishing the town’s first Hebrew school through local Zionist initiative. These may refer to different stages—the start of Hebrew classes, the founding of an organized school, or its later development—but the surviving evidence does not settle the question. It is best to preserve the discrepancy rather than choose a single founding year. ([Hebrew school](/communities/skala/records/mention_0e15be45fccab5b7fabf5312); [Tarbut School](/communities/skala/records/mention_6b9a4db257277a29d60e85e4); [first Hebrew school](/communities/skala/records/mention_18229d1c456b8b6bfb8617dc))

The book also recalls an earlier or parallel effort: the Zionist association Hashahar decided in 1906–1907 to establish an evening school for young people who wanted to study. That initiative suggests education was not only for children. It was also a way for youth to acquire learning outside the ordinary school day, in a community where Jewish education took several forms.

## More than one kind of Jewish education

The memorial book describes a layered educational landscape. Children attended the town’s Polish public school; children from traditional families also studied in *heder* or the community Talmud Torah, while those from more “enlightened” households attended the Hebrew Tarbut school. A small number continued to secondary schools outside Skala. These were not interchangeable institutions: they reflect different educational needs and outlooks within the Jewish community. The book’s account presents them as coexisting parts of local life, even as families made different choices.

The wider history helps explain why a Hebrew school mattered. Tarbut became a network of Hebrew-language schools in interwar Poland and other parts of Eastern Europe. Its institutions could include kindergartens, elementary and secondary classes, adult courses, libraries and teacher training. Skala’s school—with a kindergarten and classes described as including advanced or secondary instruction—fits that broader pattern, though its particular history must be taken from the town’s own memorial testimony, not inferred from the network alone. ([Tarbut movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarbut))

Hebrew education also had deeper roots in Galicia. The Habsburg monarchy introduced compulsory elementary schooling in 1774, while Jewish communities and reformers developed their own educational institutions; the YIVO Encyclopedia notes that Yosef Perl founded a Haskalah school in Tarnopol in 1813. This regional background does not establish a direct institutional link to Skala, but it shows that Jewish schooling in the area had long involved negotiation among state education, religious learning and modern Jewish educational projects. ([YIVO Encyclopedia, “Normalschulen”](https://yivoencyclopedia.org/article/169))

## Teachers who brought Hebrew into public life

In the memorial book, teachers emerge as the school’s defining strength. It names Roiz, Lederman, Ochshorn and Tepper among the admired educators. Chaim Roiz, also rendered as Ruiz in some records, is remembered as an outstanding teacher who won the respect of the community and the affection of hundreds of pupils. The book connects him with the Safa Brura school and with the Tarbut school; it also says he came to Skala from Peltshin, where his father, Rabbi Moshe Zalibah, was a local religious authority. It recalls Roiz’s early activity in Young Zion and his eventual migration to the Land of Israel. These details sketch a life joining education, Zionist organizing and migration, though they do not provide a full biography. ([Chaim Roiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_74c8dca0ed2de9f95a4c71be); [Safa Brura School](/communities/skala/records/mention_e0ad6fdb01d06437a0f34ad2); [Peltshin](/communities/skala/records/mention_e6b426aecbf7a5204b8cedee); [Moshe Zalibah](/communities/skala/records/mention_1a50a5e46a771f80c7503de3); [Young Zion](/communities/skala/records/mention_2e90a8f6015fa64e50190338))

The book also remembers Shraga Oksahorn—spelled in variant forms in the records—as a teacher and school leader. It describes him as a young educator who opened up the riches of Hebrew language and literature to his pupils. Lederman, Taper or Tepper, and Ruiz appear among the other teachers. The record’s different spellings caution against treating every form as a separate person; the accounts point to a circle of educators whose work gave the school its reputation. ([Shraga Oksahorn](/communities/skala/records/mention_5af4d592863fd4fd2db9f65c); [Ruiz](/communities/skala/records/mention_de8be8c7e79da8294cc9ca4e); [Oksahorn](/communities/skala/records/mention_c2c32cc8444ddb753af281b2))

The school’s influence reached beyond its pupils. According to the book, teachers and kindergarten staff organized cultural evenings, literary gatherings and theatre performed in Hebrew. The language was heard in Skala’s streets and homes. That memory suggests the school helped make Hebrew a public cultural practice, not simply a classroom subject. Deborah (Dora) Zandner is named among its pupils, one individual reminder that the institution’s story belongs not only to its teachers and organizers but also to the children who learned there. ([Deborah (Dora) Zandner](/communities/skala/records/mention_4486f8f93bebfff9a3271031))

## Bet-Am: a home for learning and community

The school’s physical home was Bet-Am, the “People’s House,” a three-story building established in 1921, according to the memorial book’s account. It brought education together with other communal activities: classrooms, a library and reading room, a large auditorium, and a basement meeting place used by Hashomer Hatzair. The building made the school part of a wider civic and cultural center. Moshe Weidberg is remembered for giving particular effort to the Tarbut school and helping build Bet-Am; the book says he later perished in the Holocaust. ([People’s House](/communities/skala/records/mention_864b36e478be14ec9df05ebd); [Moshe Weidberg](/communities/skala/records/mention_d5ef26437965bc859b244c64))

The memorial book also describes sustained community support. It credits Moshe Weidberg and other local leaders with building the institution, names Freifelder as a guardian of the Hebrew school, and recalls the women’s association approving monthly financial assistance of ten dollars. The record names Eida Wiesental and Hannah Harnik in connection with that support. Elsewhere, it remembers the narrator’s father as helping restore the Hebrew school and establish a community center. The evidence presents support as collective work, carried by organizers, donors and families—not simply an achievement of the teaching staff. ([Freifelder](/communities/skala/records/mention_e755ea482376d3a9867d80a0); [the narrator’s father](/communities/skala/records/mention_a6aa9c9948ece0651f6e1f67); [Motya Vidberg](/communities/skala/records/mention_f212f759b1c313f4e0f4fec5))

## A remembered achievement—and its limits

The book remembers Bet-Am’s library as holding about 5,000 books, in Yiddish, Polish, Hebrew and German. Its collection and the school’s cultural activities evoke a community in which Hebrew learning existed alongside other languages and traditions. A later account of Skala in the same memorial book contrasts the town with neighboring Borshchiv, saying Skala had a notable Tarbut school, Hebrew library, youth movements and Hebrew cultural events. That comparison is valuable as community memory, not an independently verified measure of educational quality.

The school’s history ended amid the destruction of Jewish life during the Second World War. The memorial testimony preserves what the community built and what it valued; it cannot, by itself, follow every pupil, teacher or relative through the upheavals that followed. What it does make clear is that Hebrew education in Skala rested on many hands: teachers such as Roiz and Oksahorn, organizers such as Vidber and Weidberg, supporters including the women’s association, and students who carried Hebrew beyond the schoolroom. The school was central not because it stood alone, but because it connected learning with language, culture and communal belonging.
